articles.title: Reform UK councillors reject proposed allowance increase
articles.excerpt: The Reform UK councillor group on Rochdale Borough Council has formally rejected a proposed increase in councillor allowances, with every group member notifying the council’s governance team that they will not accept any additional payout.
articles.content_html:
The Reform UK councillor group on Rochdale Borough Council has formally rejected a proposed increase in councillor allowances, with every group member notifying the council’s governance team that they will not accept any additional payout.

The controversial increase was rubber-stamped by Labour councillors present at the full council meeting on Thursday 16 July, with every single Labour member in attendance voting in favour. In contrast, Reform UK councillors voted unanimously against the motion, while other political groups on the council either abstained or voted against. At a time when local residents continue to face significant cost-of-living pressures and squeezed household budgets, the Reform UK group believes it is entirely wrong to increase politician payouts funded by the taxpayer. Each Reform UK councillor has now individually written to council officers to officially opt out of the increase, ensuring the extra funds remain in the public purse.

Speaking on behalf of the Reform UK group, Group Leader Councillor John Taylor said: "Hard-working families across Rochdale are having to make tough financial decisions every single day. The idea that local politicians should push through an increase in their own allowances—as Labour did at the full council meeting on 16 July—is completely out of touch with reality. We were elected to serve our community, not to line our own pockets. Reform UK voted against this increase in the chamber, and every single member of our group has now formally instructed council governance that we will refuse to take a single extra penny. We urge councillors from other parties to do the right thing and follow our lead." Reform UK remains committed to promoting financial responsibility, cutting waste in local government, and ensuring council resources are spent directly on frontline public services for the people of Rochdale.

articles.title: Reform's strongest showing yet reshapes Greater Manchester politics
articles.excerpt: Labour retained the Greater Manchester mayoralty, but Reform UK's strongest regional performance to date has reshaped the political landscape and established the party as the city's principal opposition force.
articles.content_html:
Greater Manchester has elected a new mayor, with Labour's Bev Craig succeeding Andy Burnham after winning the mayoral by-election. While Labour retained the office, one of the election's defining stories was the emergence of Reform UK as the city's principal opposition force, with Sian Astley delivering the party's strongest performance in a Greater Manchester-wide contest to date.

Craig secured 309,525 votes in the final round, representing 66.3 per cent of the vote, while Reform UK's Sian Astley received 157,178 votes, or 33.7 per cent. The result followed a second-round count after no candidate achieved an outright majority of first-preference votes.

Astley's campaign marked a significant moment for Reform UK in Greater Manchester. Standing on a platform centred on neighbourhood policing, transparency in regional government, public spending and directing more investment towards towns across all ten boroughs, she introduced the party's message to hundreds of thousands of voters and established Reform as Labour's most significant electoral challenger in the city-region.

The first-preference vote illustrated that shift. Astley secured 111,928 votes, comfortably finishing ahead of every other opposition candidate. While Labour maintained its lead, Reform's result demonstrated that many voters are now looking beyond the traditional political parties, reflecting wider political changes seen across England over recent years.

The election also highlighted the scale of the challenge facing every political party in reconnecting with the electorate. Turnout was 25.14 per cent, the lowest since the Greater Manchester mayoralty was introduced in 2017. More than three quarters of eligible voters chose not to cast a ballot despite the mayor holding responsibility for transport, policing, housing, regeneration, adult education funding and significant economic investment across the region.

For many observers, that figure raises important questions about public engagement with devolved government. The office of Mayor of Greater Manchester has become one of the most influential elected positions outside Westminster, yet millions of residents continue to feel disconnected from regional politics. Whether the low turnout reflected election fatigue, limited awareness of the mayor's powers or wider political dissatisfaction will no doubt be debated in the months ahead.

Astley's campaign also carried wider historical significance. Had she been elected, she would have become the first woman to serve as the directly elected Mayor of Greater Manchester since the office was created in 2017. Although that milestone was not reached, her candidacy demonstrated the increasing diversity of those seeking senior political office within the city-region.

The campaign itself was notable for the issues it placed at the centre of debate. Reform UK argued for greater scrutiny of Combined Authority spending, more visible neighbourhood policing, improved road maintenance and stronger accountability within regional government. Labour focused on continuing the Bee Network, delivering new housing and building on the devolution settlement developed under Andy Burnham. Voters were therefore presented with two distinctly different visions for Greater Manchester's future.

For Rochdale residents, the outcome will have practical consequences regardless of political preference. The mayor oversees Greater Manchester Police through the Police and Crime Commissioner powers, shapes strategic transport investment including the Bee Network, influences regeneration funding and represents the region in negotiations with central government. Decisions taken over the next four years will directly affect communities throughout Rochdale borough.

Although Labour retains control of the mayoralty, the election demonstrated that Greater Manchester's political landscape is becoming increasingly competitive. Reform UK's performance suggests future elections may no longer be defined by a straightforward Labour contest, with Astley's campaign establishing the party as a credible challenger across much of the city-region.

Attention now turns from campaigning to governing. Bev Craig inherits responsibility for one of England's largest devolved administrations at a time of financial pressure, growing demands on public services and continuing debate over transport, policing and housing. At the same time, Reform UK leaves the campaign with increased visibility, a larger regional profile and the opportunity to build on its strongest Greater Manchester result to date ahead of future elections.

articles.title: Littleborough RUFC invites more girls to discover rugby as women's game continues to boom
articles.excerpt: Littleborough RUFC is inviting girls from Year 6 to under-18 level to try rugby this summer, as the sport continues to grow in popularity thanks to the success of England's Red Roses and increasing awareness of the physical and mental health benefits of team sport.
articles.content_html:
Littleborough Rugby Union Football Club is encouraging girls from across Rochdale borough to give rugby a try this summer, as participation in the women's and girls' game continues to grow at every level of the sport.

The club is holding open training sessions every Tuesday from 6pm until 7pm at its Rakewood Road ground in Littleborough, welcoming girls from Year 6 through to under-18 level. Organisers say there is no commitment required, with players of all abilities invited to come along, meet new friends and experience rugby in a supportive and inclusive environment.

The sessions are designed to introduce newcomers to the sport while allowing experienced players to develop their skills in a fun, welcoming atmosphere. Coaches are keen to stress that previous rugby experience is not necessary, with the emphasis firmly on enjoyment, teamwork and building confidence.

Over the past decade, girls' rugby has experienced remarkable growth across England. The Rugby Football Union has invested heavily in the women's and girls' game, with thousands more young people now playing regularly at schools and grassroots clubs. Many local clubs have expanded their junior girls' sections in response to increasing demand, creating more opportunities than ever before for young female players.

The sport has also benefited from the growing profile of the Red Roses, England's national women's rugby team. Consistently ranked among the best teams in the world, the Red Roses have inspired a new generation of players through their success on the international stage. Record-breaking attendances at Women's Six Nations matches and Rugby World Cup fixtures have demonstrated just how rapidly interest in women's rugby has grown, with elite players increasingly becoming role models for young girls considering taking up the sport.

That success at the highest level has filtered down into communities across the country. Grassroots clubs such as Littleborough RUFC have seen increasing interest from girls looking to get involved, whether for competition, fitness or simply to make new friends.

Beyond the physical benefits of exercise, rugby is widely recognised for the positive impact it can have on mental wellbeing. Taking part in team sports has been linked to reduced feelings of isolation, improved self-esteem and greater confidence, while the friendships formed through regular training and matches often provide valuable support networks for young people.

Coaches also point to the life skills rugby helps develop. Communication, resilience, leadership, discipline and respect for teammates and opponents are central values within the game, with many parents saying participation helps children grow in confidence both on and off the pitch.

The social aspect of rugby is another major attraction. Unlike many sports where players can feel under pressure from the outset, grassroots rugby clubs often place a strong emphasis on creating welcoming environments where everyone can progress at their own pace. That approach is reflected in Littleborough's message that all abilities are welcome and that there is no obligation to commit after attending a session.

The club hopes more girls from across Rochdale, Littleborough, Milnrow, Wardle and the surrounding communities will take the opportunity to experience the sport over the summer. Open training sessions allow newcomers to meet coaches and players, learn the basics and decide whether rugby is the right fit for them before the new season begins.

Training takes place every Tuesday between 6pm and 7pm at Littleborough RUFC, OL15 0AP. Girls in Year 6 through to under-18 level are invited to attend, with organisers encouraging anyone interested to simply come along and give it a go. For further information, prospective players or parents can contact Andy on 07990 744348.

As women's rugby continues to enjoy unprecedented growth across England, clubs such as Littleborough RUFC are hoping to inspire the next generation of players while demonstrating that the game offers far more than competition alone. For many young people, it can provide lasting friendships, improved wellbeing, greater confidence and the chance to become part of a thriving local sporting community.

articles.title: Peaceful Pool sessions return to Whitworth Leisure & Wellbeing Centre for SEND families
articles.excerpt: Whitworth Leisure & Wellbeing Centre is once again offering its popular Peaceful Pool sessions throughout the summer holidays, creating a calm, welcoming and sensory-friendly swimming environment for children and adults with SEND and their families.
articles.content_html:
Families across the Rossendale Valley and Rochdale borough are being invited to enjoy a quieter, more inclusive swimming experience this summer as Whitworth Leisure & Wellbeing Centre continues its popular Peaceful Pool sessions.

Designed specifically for children and adults with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), along with their families, the sessions provide a calm, judgement-free environment where everyone can relax, connect and enjoy time together at their own pace.

The initiative recognises that many families can find busy public swimming sessions overwhelming due to noise, bright lighting and sensory stimulation. Peaceful Pool aims to remove those barriers by creating an environment where participants feel comfortable, supported and included.

Sessions will take place every Thursday from 11:30am until 1:00pm throughout the six-week summer holidays.

To create a more accessible experience, the pool environment will feature reduced lighting to provide a calmer atmosphere, while sensory toys and floating aids will be available for swimmers to enjoy. Families are encouraged to use the facilities in whatever way feels right for them, whether that means swimming, playing in the water, paddling at the poolside or simply becoming familiar with the environment.

Organisers say the sessions are all about allowing people to be themselves without fear of judgement.

The promotional campaign explains that many families of children with SEND can often feel judged or cautious about how their child's behaviour may be perceived in public spaces. Peaceful Pool has therefore been designed to offer a welcoming environment where everyone can feel safe, respected and accepted.

The centre's message is simple: 'Everyone is welcome here just as you are.' That philosophy reflects a growing recognition across the leisure sector of the importance of making public facilities more inclusive and accessible for people with additional needs.

Swimming is widely recognised for its physical and mental wellbeing benefits, helping to improve confidence, mobility, coordination and overall fitness while providing an enjoyable activity for the whole family. Creating opportunities for families to access those benefits in a supportive environment can make a significant difference for many people who may otherwise struggle to attend mainstream sessions.

The Peaceful Pool sessions are available at the standard swim admission price, ensuring families can take part without paying a premium for accessible provision.

Whitworth Leisure & Wellbeing Centre continues to expand its programme of community-focused activities, with Peaceful Pool forming part of its wider commitment to ensuring local leisure facilities are welcoming and inclusive for residents of all ages and abilities.

Peaceful Pool takes place every Thursday between 11:30am and 1:00pm throughout the six-week summer holidays at Whitworth Leisure & Wellbeing Centre.

articles.title: Late-night fireworks return to Shawclough and Healey as residents' frustration grows
articles.excerpt: Residents in Shawclough and Healey have reported a second consecutive evening of fireworks after 11pm, with growing frustration over disrupted sleep, distressed pets and concerns for wildlife near Healey Dell Nature Reserve.
articles.content_html:
Residents across Shawclough and Healey have once again reported being disturbed by late-night fireworks, with explosions heard at approximately 11.21pm on Sunday evening. The latest incident marks the second consecutive night of reports, leaving many residents questioning when meaningful action will be taken to tackle the ongoing nuisance.

For many households, the issue extends far beyond a brief display. Parents have described children being woken after bedtime, pet owners report anxious and distressed animals, and residents working early shifts say repeated interruptions to their sleep are becoming increasingly difficult to tolerate.

The repeated use of fireworks late at night has also prompted renewed concerns for local wildlife. Healey Dell Nature Reserve, together with the surrounding woodland, provides important habitat for nesting birds, bats and other protected species. Wildlife organisations have long warned that unexpected loud explosions can disturb feeding, nesting and breeding behaviour, particularly during sensitive periods of the year.

Residents have increasingly questioned whether existing legislation is sufficient to prevent repeated anti-social use of fireworks. While fireworks can be legally purchased and used subject to restrictions, businesses selling them must comply with licensing and storage regulations. However, any decision to suspend or revoke a retailer's licence would require evidence that they had breached those legal requirements. Simply because fireworks are being misused by individuals does not automatically mean a retailer has acted unlawfully.

Enforcement remains difficult, particularly when fireworks are discharged from private property under the cover of darkness. Identifying those responsible often relies on witness evidence, CCTV or reports made at the time of the incident.

Nevertheless, residents say patience is wearing thin. After another evening of disrupted sleep, many are calling for stronger enforcement, tighter controls on sales and greater action against those repeatedly using fireworks in residential neighbourhoods late at night.

Fireworks remain an important part of many cultural and community celebrations when used responsibly. However, repeated displays after 11pm in quiet residential areas are a very different matter. Communities should not have to endure nightly disruption, frightened pets, exhausted children and unnecessary disturbance to local wildlife. As complaints continue to mount, many residents are asking a simple question: when will enough finally be enough?

articles.title: Shisha Lounge Closed After Carbon Monoxide Exposure
articles.excerpt: Phantom The Lounge has been shut down after a court order found excessive carbon monoxide levels posed a risk to customers and staff.
articles.content_html:
A shisha lounge in Rochdale has been closed following a court order due to dangerous levels of carbon monoxide found on the premises. Phantom The Lounge, located on Maclure Road, was ordered to cease operations by Rochdale Council's environmental health service after a routine inspection revealed serious violations of health regulations.

The closure order was granted at Manchester Magistrates' Court on July 24, based on evidence submitted by environmental health officers, with support from Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service and Greater Manchester Police. The inspection found that the lounge had been illegally operating by allowing smoking in a substantially closed area, which contravenes the Smoke-Free regulations under the Health Act 2006.

In addition to the illegal smoking, the inspection uncovered hazardous practices in the kitchen that exposed customers and staff to excessively high levels of carbon monoxide. An electric fan was reportedly used to smoulder coals in an unventilated area, resulting in carbon monoxide levels exceeding 100 parts per million (PPM) in the kitchen. On two occasions, fire officers had to instruct customers and staff to leave the premises for their safety.

Rochdale Council stated that they had offered the owners an opportunity to rectify the issues, but the business refused to cooperate. This lack of compliance led to the council's environmental health service taking court action as a last resort. Councillor Tricia Ayrton, deputy leader and portfolio holder for Climate Change and Environment, emphasised the importance of health regulations in ensuring the safety of both customers and workers.

articles.title: Fresh complaints over persistent landfill odour as Heywood residents report 'sewer' stench and fly infestation
articles.excerpt: Residents across Heywood have once again reported a strong foul odour and increasing numbers of flies, prompting renewed questions over the long-running issues surrounding the Pilsworth South landfill site.
articles.content_html:
Residents across Heywood have once again reported a strong unpleasant smell drifting across parts of the town, with many describing an odour resembling sewage, rotting waste or landfill gas. The latest complaints have reignited concerns over the long-running issues surrounding the nearby Pilsworth South landfill site.

Several residents also reported unusually high numbers of flies, a problem which campaigners have previously associated with the landfill during earlier periods of odour complaints.

Rebecca Hodkinson wrote: "Yep... Unfortunately. And the amount of flies is something else this year."

Billy Casper added: "It stunk rotten like sewers when I was walking up Heywood past Iceland at 5.30 this evening. I don't think it was the landfill though."

Jeanette Noble commented: "I've been smelling it on Darnhill for a few months and the amount of flies is terrible."

Although some residents believe the smell may have originated elsewhere, the recurrence of similar complaints has led many to question whether problems linked to the landfill have returned.

The issue first gained widespread public attention during 2024 when thousands of complaints were submitted to the Environment Agency by residents across Heywood, Middleton, Bury and Rochdale. The smell became one of the borough's most significant environmental concerns, leading to regulatory investigations into landfill gas management and odour control measures at the site.

Under environmental law, landfill sites are permitted to operate only under an Environmental Permit issued by the Environment Agency. Operators are legally required to use Best Available Techniques (BAT) to prevent or minimise pollution, including offensive odours. Persistent smells escaping beyond the site boundary are not automatically unlawful, but they can lead to regulatory enforcement where permit conditions are breached. The Environment Agency has powers to require operational improvements, vary permit conditions, or take enforcement action where appropriate.

The issue has also attracted political attention. West Heywood councillor Angela Brown has repeatedly encouraged residents to report every odour incident directly to the Environment Agency, stressing that detailed reports help investigators establish patterns and build evidence. Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has likewise raised concerns publicly and in Parliament regarding the impact of the landfill on surrounding communities.

Controversy has continued following approval for further landfill operations despite ongoing complaints from nearby residents. Campaigners argue that expansion should not proceed until odour problems have been fully resolved, while regulators maintain that environmental permits require operators to comply with strict controls.

Residents experiencing offensive odours are encouraged to report incidents directly to the Environment Agency, recording the date, time, location, weather conditions and a description of the smell. Multiple reports from different locations can assist investigators in determining whether a wider environmental incident is occurring.

For many residents, the recurring nature of the complaints is becoming increasingly frustrating. While only a full investigation can determine the source of any individual odour event, the persistence of reports over recent years demonstrates that confidence among the local community has yet to be restored.

articles.title: Editorial: Justice remains unfinished in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: More than a decade after the Rochdale grooming gang scandal shocked Britain, the perpetrators have been jailed, reforms have been introduced and institutions have apologised. Yet for many survivors and residents, questions about accountability, trust and whether justice has truly been delivered remain unanswered.
articles.content_html:
More than a decade has passed since the Rochdale child sexual exploitation scandal exposed one of the gravest safeguarding failures in modern British history. The men responsible have been convicted and imprisoned, but the question that continues to confront Rochdale is whether justice ended with those convictions.

Successive independent inquiries have reached strikingly similar conclusions. Reviews by Parliament, local safeguarding bodies and independent investigators found that vulnerable children were repeatedly failed by institutions responsible for protecting them. Victims were too often viewed as making 'lifestyle choices' rather than recognised as children subjected to coercion, rape, trafficking and organised sexual exploitation. Information was not consistently shared between agencies, warning signs were missed, organised offending was underestimated and opportunities to intervene were repeatedly lost.

The testimony of survivors remains among the most compelling evidence of those failures. Girls described repeatedly reporting abuse only to be disbelieved, dismissed as troublesome teenagers or treated as willing participants in their own exploitation. Children who regularly went missing were returned to the same environments where offenders continued to target them. Independent reviews concluded that professionals frequently focused on victims' behaviour rather than the methods of coercion used by organised offenders.

The criminal justice system eventually delivered significant convictions. Operation Span resulted in nine men being convicted in 2012 for offences including rape, trafficking and conspiracy to engage in sexual activity with children. Further investigations have led to additional prosecutions linked to historic child sexual exploitation across Greater Manchester. Judges described the offending as calculated, organised and profoundly damaging, recognising that many victims would carry lifelong psychological trauma.

Yet convictions answered only one question: the guilt of the offenders. They did not answer why children were repeatedly failed before those prosecutions ever reached a courtroom.

The official inquiries found that the primary problem was not an absence of legislation. The criminal offences already existed. Rather, agencies failed to recognise organised grooming, safeguarding procedures were inconsistently applied, intelligence was not always effectively shared and vulnerable children were too often judged instead of protected. Some reviews also concluded that concerns about community tensions influenced professional decision-making in certain cases, although they stressed that institutional failures were complex and involved multiple contributing factors.

Political debate over those failures continues today. Sir Keir Starmer has consistently defended his record as Director of Public Prosecutions, pointing to reforms introduced after the Rochdale prosecutions that encouraged prosecutors to focus more closely on suspect behaviour rather than relying heavily on assessments of victim credibility. Nigel Farage has repeatedly argued that institutional accountability remains incomplete and has called for wider national inquiries into organised child sexual exploitation.

Independent MP Rupert Lowe commissioned his own inquiry into grooming gangs, arguing that previous investigations had failed to provide full transparency or accountability. Lowe's report calls for mandatory recording of offender ethnicity, stronger criminal justice responses, improved national data collection and further investigation into institutional failings. While his inquiry does not carry statutory authority, it has become part of the continuing national debate surrounding organised child sexual exploitation and institutional responsibility.

London Mayor Sadiq Khan also faced criticism after asking for clarification during a London Assembly meeting about what was meant by the phrase 'grooming gangs' before responding more broadly on child sexual exploitation. The exchange became part of the wider political discussion over how public authorities describe organised abuse and communicate with victims and the public.

There have unquestionably been improvements since the original scandal. Greater Manchester Police has established dedicated child sexual exploitation capabilities, multi-agency safeguarding arrangements have been strengthened, inspection reports have recognised improvements in identifying vulnerable children and historic offenders continue to face prosecution years after their crimes. Those reforms are significant and should not be dismissed.

However, reform is not the same as accountability.

For many survivors, organisational apologies and revised procedures have never fully addressed the institutional failures identified by successive inquiries. Former Greater Manchester Police detective Maggie Oliver has repeatedly argued that child sexual exploitation remains a continuing threat and has warned against believing the lessons of Rochdale have been fully learned. She has consistently maintained that safeguarding depends not only on procedures but on professionals who are prepared to challenge assumptions, recognise organised exploitation and place children's welfare above institutional reputation.

Child sexual exploitation has not disappeared. Police forces across England and Wales continue to investigate organised grooming offences while offenders increasingly exploit social media, encrypted messaging platforms, online coercion and county lines criminality. Organised abuse evolves. Safeguarding must evolve with it.

The greatest lesson from Rochdale is not that Britain lacked the legal powers to prosecute offenders. It is that institutions repeatedly failed to use those powers when vulnerable children first asked for help. Children who should have been believed were doubted. Warning signs that should have triggered intervention were overlooked. Opportunities to prevent further abuse were lost.

Rochdale Borough Council has acknowledged profound institutional failings and apologised to survivors. Public bodies have accepted that serious mistakes were made, while successive reforms have sought to strengthen safeguarding and improve inter-agency cooperation. Those changes deserve recognition.

Whether they have fully restored public trust is another question entirely.

Justice cannot be measured solely by the length of prison sentences imposed on offenders. It is also measured by whether institutions learn from catastrophic failure, whether public officials accept responsibility when safeguarding collapses and whether every vulnerable child reporting abuse today can expect to be believed, protected and acted upon without hesitation.

Until survivors believe those standards have been achieved, and until the public is confident that institutional accountability carries meaningful consequences as well as organisational reform, many will continue to conclude that justice in Rochdale remains unfinished.

articles.title: Labour Wins GM Election: a narrow mandate, a continuity platform, and a borough still waiting
articles.excerpt: Bev Craig is Mayor of Greater Manchester, elected on the lowest turnout the office has seen and taken to a second round by Reform.
articles.content_html:
Bev Craig takes office as Mayor of Greater Manchester having won 309,525 votes to Sian Astley's 157,178, a second-round margin of 66.3 per cent to 33.7. She inherits transport, policing, housing and skills powers assembled over nine years, and a budget running to billions.

Turnout was 25.14 per cent, the lowest since the office was created. Craig's total amounts to roughly one in seven of those entitled to vote. That is not a criticism of her — she did not choose the date, and no candidate can compel people to the polls. But it could set the stage for what follows. A mayor with powers of this scale and a base of active consent this narrow should expect close questioning, and would be wise to welcome it.

The contest was also tighter on first preferences than the final figure implies. Neither candidate reached 50 per cent outright, which is why a second count was needed. Reform UK finished second across all ten boroughs at its first serious attempt at this office. Labour has held the mayoralty since it was created; it has now been taken to a second round in its strongest English region.

The substantive disagreement is about continuity. Craig campaigned on carrying forward the programme she inherits — the Bee Network, housing delivery, neighbourhood policing, further devolution talks with government. For Manchester that is a reasonable prospectus. For Rochdale it is the least attractive offer available, because the arrangement now being continued has not worked here. The borough sits at the end of a Metrolink line, with a rail service that has been unreliable for years, contributing to a city-region strategy whose most visible results are concentrated closer to the centre.

There is a fair answer to that, and it deserves stating. Craig's supporters argue that a Labour mayor working with a Labour government is better placed to win further devolved powers and the money attached to them, and that Rochdale gains more from that than from opposition. It is a serious argument. It is also a testable one, and the test is whether the borough's share of transport and housing investment rises over the next four years or stays where it is.

On policing, the mayor holds the powers of a Police and Crime Commissioner, which makes this the area where the office touches residents most directly. Our measure will be simple and public: response times, charge rates, and whether people who report a crime in this borough hear back. Those figures are published. We intend to use them.

The by-election itself carried a cost — the 2024 mayoral contest cost taxpayers £4.7 million, and this one is expected to run to millions again. That is a consequence of a sitting mayor leaving mid-term for Westminster, not of anything the new mayor did. But it is money spent on an election in which three quarters of the electorate did not participate, and it is reasonable to ask what the region got for it.

Craig begins with substantial powers and a quiet electorate. We will report what she does with them, and judge her on what changes in this borough rather than on what is announced in Manchester.

articles.title: Everything You Need to Know Before Rochdale Feel Good Festival 2026
articles.excerpt: From headliners and ticket prices to travel, parking, accessibility and the latest weather forecast, here's everything you need to know before Rochdale Feel Good Festival returns next weekend.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale's biggest annual music event returns next weekend, with thousands of visitors expected to descend on the town centre for the 2026 Feel Good Festival. Headlined by BRIT Award-winning singer Gabrielle, alongside indie favourites Ash and Starsailor, the festival promises a full day of live music, street entertainment, food, drink and family activities, continuing a tradition that has become one of Greater Manchester's most successful free town centre festivals.

Now celebrating its 15th edition, the Feel Good Festival has grown from a small local music event into one of the highlights of the borough's cultural calendar. Previous festivals have welcomed acts including Ocean Colour Scene, Razorlight, Feeder, The Coral, Scouting For Girls, The Fratellis, Heather Small, Cast, Toploader, Badly Drawn Boy, The Feeling, The Lightning Seeds and The Beat, attracting visitors from across the North West and providing a welcome boost to Rochdale's hospitality and retail sectors.

This year's main stage takes place in the stunning surroundings of the newly restored Rochdale Town Hall Square on Saturday, 8 August. Headlining the evening is Gabrielle, whose catalogue includes classics such as Dreams, Rise and Out of Reach. She is joined by Ash, Starsailor, funk and soul outfit The Allergies and Manchester indie rising star Alex Spencer, with additional performances throughout the day and live entertainment continuing across numerous indoor venues around the town centre. Most indoor performances remain completely free, with only the main stage requiring a ticket.

Festival organisers have continued their commitment to making the event affordable. Early bird tickets sold out quickly at £15 before subsequent release phases increased to £25, £30, £35 and the final allocation at £45 plus booking fees. VIP upgrades remain available for those wanting premium viewing areas and additional hospitality. Every ticket includes a reusable festival cup as part of the organisers' ongoing efforts to reduce single-use plastics.

Entertainment begins from 11.30am and continues until approximately 10.45pm, with the main stage located in Rochdale Town Hall Square. Festival organisers recommend arriving early to collect wristbands, avoid queues and enjoy the wide variety of free entertainment taking place throughout the town centre before the headline performances begin.

Getting to the festival is expected to be straightforward thanks to Rochdale's excellent public transport links. Organisers are encouraging visitors to use public transport where possible, with Metrolink trams running directly into Rochdale town centre and Northern train services providing regular connections from Manchester Victoria, Leeds, Halifax and Blackburn. Numerous Bee Network bus services also stop within a short walk of the festival site, while taxi ranks will operate throughout the day and into the evening to assist those travelling home after the headline acts.

Drivers are advised to allow extra time, as town centre car parks are expected to fill quickly. Public parking is available at several locations including The Esplanade, Riverside, Baillie Street and other nearby council-operated car parks, although temporary road closures around the Town Hall may affect access during the festival. Visitors are encouraged to check council travel advice before setting off.

Accessibility continues to be a major focus for organisers. A dedicated accessible viewing platform will be available within the main stage arena for wheelchair users and those with mobility issues, while British Sign Language interpreters will be present during main stage performances. Accessible toilets are provided both within the outdoor festival site and nearby indoor venues. Essential companion tickets are available free of charge for eligible visitors, assistance dogs are welcome and a quiet space will also be available for anyone requiring time away from the crowds.

Toilets will be located throughout the festival site, including accessible facilities, with additional public conveniences available inside participating venues. Festival stewards will be on hand throughout the day to assist visitors and provide directions around the event.

Food has become almost as popular as the music in recent years, with dozens of traders expected to serve everything from gourmet burgers and wood-fired pizzas to Asian street food, desserts and locally produced refreshments. Although organisers have not published official bar prices, visitors should expect festival-standard pricing broadly comparable with similar outdoor events across Greater Manchester. Outside alcohol is not permitted inside the main stage arena, although sealed soft drinks and water may be allowed subject to festival rules. Visitors are encouraged to support local independent food and drink traders operating throughout the event.

The weather currently looks favourable for festival-goers, with forecasts suggesting a mostly sunny day, light winds and temperatures reaching around 19°C. While conditions can always change, current forecasts indicate comfortable weather for spending the day outdoors, although organisers still recommend bringing sunscreen, drinking plenty of water and packing a light waterproof just in case the British summer has other ideas.

Beyond the music, the Feel Good Festival has become an important economic event for Rochdale. Thousands of visitors pass through the town centre every year, providing a significant boost to local restaurants, pubs, cafés, hotels and independent retailers. The festival also showcases Rochdale's cultural offer following the restoration of the Grade I-listed Town Hall and supports the borough's wider ambitions to attract more visitors and investment.

The festival is organised on behalf of Rochdale Borough Council with support from Rochdale Development Agency, ticket sales and sponsorship from local businesses and community partners. Over the years, numerous organisations have supported the event, helping to ensure it remains one of the North West's best-value music festivals while continuing to celebrate local talent alongside nationally recognised artists.

For anyone planning to attend, organisers recommend arriving early, using public transport where possible, checking travel updates before setting off and allowing extra time to move between venues. Whether you're there to see Gabrielle, discover new artists, enjoy the food village or simply soak up the atmosphere in Rochdale town centre, this year's Feel Good Festival looks set to continue one of the borough's proudest summer traditions.

articles.title: Residents in Shawclough and Healey call for action over late-night fireworks
articles.excerpt: Residents in Shawclough and Healey are calling for stronger action after repeated late-night fireworks disrupted neighbourhoods, with concerns over sleep, vulnerable people, wildlife and the difficulty of identifying those responsible.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Shawclough and Healey are calling for stronger action after repeated late-night fireworks disturbed neighbourhoods, with many saying explosions after 11pm are affecting sleep, frightening children and causing distress to vulnerable people. While organised displays remain an important part of celebrations throughout the year, many residents say fireworks are increasingly being let off on ordinary evenings with little regard for those living nearby.

The latest complaints prompted a strong response on social media. Local resident Nick Simpson wrote: "Absolutely outrageous. These people need to be locked up and fined," reflecting frustration shared by others who say the disturbances have become an unwelcome feature of late evenings.

Councillor Shah Wazir also urged residents to report incidents wherever possible. Responding to complaints, he said: "Please report this to police and if you know the address then it will certainly help. Firework at night is totally unacceptable, no matter what occasion."

Fireworks are already regulated by law. In most circumstances they cannot legally be set off between 11pm and 7am, with later cut-off times applying only on Bonfire Night, New Year's Eve, Diwali and Chinese New Year. Retailers can only sell fireworks all year if they hold the appropriate licence, while most other retailers are restricted to seasonal sales.

Despite those laws, many residents believe enforcement remains one of the biggest challenges. Fireworks are usually set off after dark from private gardens, alleyways or open spaces, making it difficult for neighbours to identify exactly where they have come from. By the time officers could arrive, the noise has often stopped and those responsible may have left the area.

Many people are also understandably reluctant to confront those responsible themselves. Approaching unknown individuals late at night carries obvious risks, particularly where alcohol or antisocial behaviour may already be involved. Residents say they often feel they have little practical option beyond reporting incidents after they have happened, despite recognising that successful enforcement depends on accurate information.

The disruption extends far beyond a few loud bangs. Parents describe young children being startled awake and struggling to settle again, while elderly residents and people recovering from illness can lose valuable sleep. Mental health charities have also highlighted the impact unexpected fireworks can have on people living with anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder and other conditions where sudden loud noises may trigger distress.

Wildlife is also affected. Conservation organisations have warned that repeated fireworks can disturb nesting birds and protected species such as bats, while many pet owners report dogs, cats and other animals becoming frightened by sudden explosions. Unlike organised displays, fireworks used without warning leave residents with little opportunity to prepare vulnerable family members or animals.

The issue has prompted wider debate over whether existing laws go far enough or whether stronger enforcement is needed. While legislation already restricts when fireworks can be used, many residents argue the difficulty lies in identifying those responsible quickly enough for police to take effective action.

Greater Manchester Police encourages anyone witnessing the illegal use of fireworks or persistent antisocial behaviour to report it, particularly where an address or precise location can be provided. As concerns continue to emerge from Shawclough, Healey and other parts of the borough, many residents hope greater awareness, responsible use and more effective enforcement will help restore quieter evenings to Rochdale's neighbourhoods.

articles.title: Is ketamine becoming a problem in Rochdale? Health leaders warn of a growing concern
articles.excerpt: Health professionals are warning of the growing harms associated with ketamine as national use rises. But what does the picture look like in Rochdale, and why are experts becoming increasingly concerned?
articles.content_html:
Ketamine was once regarded primarily as a nightclub drug, but health professionals, police and addiction specialists say its use has changed dramatically over the past decade. Increasingly, the drug is being used by younger people in a wider range of settings, prompting growing concern about its impact on physical and mental health.

While there is no publicly available evidence to suggest Rochdale has a ketamine problem significantly worse than other parts of Greater Manchester, local authorities recognise substance misuse as an important public health issue and have included drug-related harm as a key priority in the borough's long-term prevention strategy. Rochdale's Preventing Drug and Alcohol Harm Strategy highlights the need to reduce drug-related harm through prevention, early intervention, treatment and recovery services.

Ketamine is a Class B controlled drug in the UK. Originally developed as a medical anaesthetic, it produces feelings of detachment and hallucinations when used recreationally. In recent years, it has become increasingly popular because it is often cheaper than cocaine and MDMA, while users mistakenly believe it to be a 'safer' drug.

National evidence suggests that perception is dangerously wrong. The Home Office's latest wastewater analysis estimates ketamine consumption has increased substantially in England in recent years, making it one of the country's most commonly consumed illegal drugs after cocaine.

Doctors are particularly concerned about the long-term physical effects. Repeated ketamine use can cause irreversible damage to the bladder and urinary tract, a condition sometimes referred to as 'ketamine bladder' or ketamine-induced cystitis. Heavy users may experience severe pain, frequent urination, bleeding and, in the most serious cases, permanent bladder damage requiring reconstructive surgery. Medical specialists have reported a significant increase in young patients requiring treatment for these complications.

Mental health professionals also warn that regular ketamine use can lead to dependency, memory problems, anxiety, depression and episodes of psychosis in some individuals. Because the drug affects perception and coordination, users are also at increased risk of accidents, injuries and dangerous behaviour while intoxicated.

Locally, Rochdale Borough Council's Joint Strategic Needs Assessment identifies substance misuse among young adults as an ongoing public health challenge. Hospital admission rates linked to substance misuse among young people remain broadly similar to the national average, while the council notes that vulnerable groups are at greater risk of developing drug-related problems.

Although official figures are not routinely broken down by individual drug at borough level, professionals working in addiction services across Greater Manchester say ketamine now features far more frequently than it did a decade ago. Nationally, the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs concluded earlier this year that misuse is increasing and recommended strengthening education, prevention and treatment services while keeping ketamine as a Class B drug.

Parents are encouraged to be aware of the warning signs. These can include sudden mood changes, poor concentration, unexplained urinary problems, nosebleeds caused by snorting powder, secrecy around friendships, declining school or college attendance and unexplained financial difficulties. None of these signs alone necessarily indicate drug use, but experts advise early conversations and support where concerns exist.

Support is available for anyone struggling with drug use. Rochdale residents can access confidential help through local drug and alcohol treatment services without fear of judgement. Health professionals stress that seeking support early greatly improves the chances of recovery and helps prevent long-term physical damage.

The message from health leaders is clear. While ketamine may still carry an image as a recreational party drug, the evidence increasingly shows it can have devastating consequences for both physical and mental health. Prevention, education and early intervention remain the most effective ways of protecting young people across Rochdale borough from the lasting harm associated with its misuse.

articles.title: Discover the beauty on your doorstep: The spectacular walks of Shawclough and Healey
articles.excerpt: From Healey Dell to the Pennine moors, Shawclough and Healey offer some of Greater Manchester's finest walking routes. Here's how to enjoy them responsibly while discovering the wildlife and landscapes on your doorstep.
articles.content_html:
With rolling moorland, ancient woodland, dramatic valleys and panoramic Pennine views, Shawclough and Healey offer some of the finest walking routes anywhere in Greater Manchester. Just a few minutes from Rochdale town centre, the area provides easy access to miles of public footpaths, bridleways and countryside that attract walkers, runners, cyclists and nature lovers throughout the year.

Whether you're looking for a gentle afternoon stroll or a challenging hike onto the South Pennine moors, there is a route to suit every ability. Healey Dell Nature Reserve remains one of the area's most popular destinations, with its historic railway viaduct, woodland trails and the River Spodden winding through a picturesque valley rich in wildlife. From there, walkers can continue towards Shawclough, Rooley Moor Road, Brown Wardle Hill, Knowl Hill and the Pennine Bridleway, enjoying some of the most impressive views across Rochdale, Rossendale and beyond. The wider area also links into the Rochdale Way and Rossendale Way, providing opportunities for much longer circular walks.

The landscape changes dramatically with the seasons. During late summer, the surrounding moorland is coloured by flowering heather, while ancient dry stone walls, reservoirs and grazing farmland create the classic Pennine scenery that has inspired walkers for generations.

The area is also a haven for wildlife. At this time of year, walkers are likely to spot kestrels hovering above the fields, buzzards circling on thermals, swallows and house martins feeding before beginning their autumn migration, and flocks of goldfinches gathering on seed heads. In the woodlands around Healey Dell, visitors may hear great spotted woodpeckers, nuthatches, wrens, robins and tawny owls after dusk. Lucky walkers may even catch sight of kingfishers along quieter stretches of the River Spodden. Roe deer are regularly seen at dawn and dusk around Healey Dell, Rooley Moor and neighbouring farmland, while foxes, badgers, rabbits and brown hares also inhabit the surrounding countryside.

As enjoyable as these walks are, visitors are reminded that much of the surrounding countryside remains working farmland. Public Rights of Way allow people to cross private land using designated footpaths and bridleways, but walkers should always remain on the marked route unless they are on land with wider access rights. Respecting the Countryside Code helps ensure these routes remain open for everyone to enjoy.

Simple acts of courtesy make a significant difference. Gates should always be left exactly as they are found. If a gate is closed, close it again after passing through. If it has been left open, leave it open. Farmers often manage livestock carefully, and an incorrectly opened or closed gate can allow animals to stray or separate livestock.

Dog owners also have an important responsibility. Even the friendliest dog can frighten livestock, particularly sheep with lambs or cattle with calves. Dogs should be kept under close control and, wherever livestock are present, they should be kept on a lead. If cattle become inquisitive or begin approaching, it is usually safest to release the dog if necessary, as it can outrun livestock and return once the danger has passed.

Walkers are also encouraged to remain vigilant for injured or distressed animals. If you discover a sheep that has rolled onto its back and cannot get up—a situation known as being 'cast' or 'turned over'—or encounter injured cattle, the best course of action is to contact the farmer if they can be identified, or report the location to the local authority or police if there is an immediate welfare concern. Unless you are experienced and it is safe to do so, avoid attempting to handle large livestock yourself.

The natural beauty of Shawclough and Healey depends on everyone doing their part. Taking litter home, avoiding lighting fires, respecting wildlife and staying on established paths all help protect this special landscape for future generations.

For many residents, one of the greatest pleasures of living in Rochdale is having countryside of this quality virtually on the doorstep. In less than an hour, it is possible to walk from peaceful woodland to open Pennine moorland, passing historic landmarks, abundant wildlife and breathtaking viewpoints along the way.

As summer gradually gives way to autumn, there are few better times to lace up your walking boots, head for the hills and rediscover the remarkable countryside that surrounds Shawclough and Healey.

articles.title: Rochdale-born TikToker investigated by Scottish police over Meta smart glasses videos
articles.excerpt: A Rochdale-born TikTok creator known online as 'E Dobbin' is being investigated by Scottish police after complaints relating to videos recorded using Meta smart glasses.
articles.content_html:
Scott Margerison, a Rochdale native who publishes content online under the alias 'E Dobbin', is being investigated by Scottish police following complaints about videos allegedly recorded using Meta smart glasses during a trip around Scotland.

According to the Daily Record, officers are reviewing footage to determine whether any criminal offences have been committed. The reported videos include members of the public, retail staff and CalMac employees being recorded, along with confrontational interactions and footage from the bridge of the CalMac ferry Loch Seaforth. CalMac subsequently suspended public bridge visits.

Previous controversies

The Scotland investigation is not the first controversy surrounding Margerison's online activity. He previously attracted significant public criticism after uploading footage filmed inside JD Gym in which viewers alleged he made racist and sexually explicit remarks while recording members of the public. Reports at the time indicated he was subsequently banned from the gym.

Online content

Across multiple TikTok accounts, some of which are no longer available, Margerison has published videos promoting numerous conspiracy theories and alternative historical claims. These include the Tartaria conspiracy theory, claims that the Apollo Moon landings were faked, the so-called Kalergi Plan conspiracy theory, and claims that mountains are the fossilised remains of enormous petrified creatures.

The Kalergi Plan conspiracy theory has been widely rejected by historians and researchers and is commonly associated with antisemitic conspiracy narratives.

Many of Margerison's videos challenge established historical, archaeological and scientific consensus and have generated substantial debate and criticism online.

Police investigation

Scottish police have confirmed officers received complaints and are reviewing the available material to establish whether any criminal offences have been committed.

At the time of publication no criminal charges have been announced. An investigation does not imply criminal guilt.

articles.title: After Burnham: What the Next Mayor Inherits
articles.excerpt: The next Mayor of Greater Manchester will inherit far more than Andy Burnham's office, taking responsibility for one of England's most powerful devolved administrations at a time of political and financial change.
articles.content_html:
Whoever becomes the next Mayor of Greater Manchester will inherit one of the most powerful devolved political offices in England at a pivotal moment for both the city-region and national politics. Andy Burnham's departure after almost nine years in office marks the end of an era that saw the mayoralty evolve from a relatively new experiment in devolution into a position with significant influence over transport, policing, regeneration, housing and economic development.

Burnham's resignation to return to Westminster has inevitably altered the political landscape. During his time as mayor he became synonymous with Greater Manchester's devolution agenda, frequently acting as the public face of the region during negotiations with successive governments. Whether residents agreed with his policies or not, few would dispute that he raised the national profile of Greater Manchester and demonstrated how influential a metro mayor could become.

The incoming mayor therefore faces a different challenge from Burnham in 2017. Rather than creating the office's identity from scratch, the next incumbent must decide whether to build on Burnham's approach or chart a new direction. Expectations are considerably higher than they were nine years ago because the public now expects the mayor to deliver visible improvements rather than simply establish the role.

Transport remains the most obvious priority. The Bee Network has become one of the flagship achievements of Greater Manchester's devolution settlement, bringing buses back under public control and integrating services with trams and active travel. While supporters argue that the network is beginning to create a genuinely joined-up public transport system, critics continue to raise concerns about reliability, congestion, funding and the pace of implementation. The next mayor will inherit both the opportunities and the political scrutiny that accompany such an ambitious programme.

Policing is another area where expectations remain high. The Mayor of Greater Manchester also exercises the powers of the Police and Crime Commissioner, giving the office direct responsibility for setting policing priorities, overseeing budgets and holding Greater Manchester Police to account. Crime, antisocial behaviour and neighbourhood policing featured prominently throughout the by-election campaign, with candidates from across the political spectrum promising safer communities, stronger visible policing and better support for victims.

Housing and regeneration are likely to remain central themes throughout the next mayoral term. Greater Manchester continues to experience significant demand for affordable housing while balancing pressures for economic growth, environmental protection and infrastructure investment. Large regeneration schemes are transforming parts of Manchester city centre, Salford and several surrounding boroughs, but many communities continue to ask whether the benefits of that growth are being shared equally across the region.

For Rochdale, those questions are particularly important. Investment decisions made by the combined authority influence transport links, skills funding, brownfield regeneration, town centre renewal and wider economic development. Although individual councils retain many planning responsibilities, the mayor plays a significant strategic role in shaping investment priorities across Greater Manchester.

The constitutional picture is also changing. Devolution has steadily expanded over the past decade, with successive governments transferring additional responsibilities from Whitehall to regional authorities. Greater Manchester has often been used as the model for further devolution elsewhere in England, meaning decisions taken by its mayor frequently attract national attention. The incoming mayor is therefore likely to spend as much time negotiating with ministers as delivering local policy.

The by-election campaigns reflected differing views about how those powers should be exercised. Labour argued for continuity, seeking to build on existing transport and regeneration programmes. Reform UK focused on reducing public spending, increasing accountability and prioritising crime and community safety. Restore Britain centred its campaign on transparency, democratic reform and greater public involvement in local decision-making. The Conservatives promoted business growth and improved public services, while the Green Party emphasised sustainability and environmental investment. Liberal Democrats highlighted local accountability and public service reform. Although their policies differed considerably, almost every candidate accepted that the mayoralty has become one of the region's most influential political offices.

Another challenge awaiting the successful candidate is rebuilding public engagement. The record-low turnout has inevitably raised questions about democratic participation. While the mayor's powers have expanded significantly since 2017, public awareness has not always kept pace. Many residents still struggle to distinguish between the responsibilities of local councils, Parliament and the combined authority. Improving understanding of what the mayor actually does may become almost as important as delivering new policies.

Financial pressures will also shape the next administration. Like councils across England, Greater Manchester faces difficult decisions over public spending. Rising demand for public services, inflationary pressures and competing investment priorities mean every major project will come under close scrutiny. The next mayor will need to balance long-term ambitions with short-term financial realities while maintaining public confidence.

Perhaps the greatest test, however, will be leadership. Andy Burnham's tenure demonstrated that a metro mayor can become a nationally recognised political figure capable of influencing debates far beyond the boundaries of Greater Manchester. His successor now inherits not only extensive powers but also heightened expectations. Residents will judge the next mayor not simply by campaign promises but by whether transport improves, neighbourhoods feel safer, regeneration reaches towns beyond Manchester city centre and economic growth benefits communities across all ten boroughs.

The constitutional significance of this transition should not be underestimated. For the first time since the office was created, Greater Manchester is entering a post-Burnham era. Whether that represents continuity or a fresh chapter will depend not only on the election result but on how effectively the next mayor uses one of the most powerful devolved mandates in the country. The office has matured; now its next occupant must prove that devolution itself can continue to deliver meaningful change for the people it was designed to serve.

articles.title: Brass band tradition returns to Hare Hill Park this September
articles.excerpt: Friends of Hare Hill Park are inviting residents to enjoy a free afternoon of brass band music on 6 September, celebrating one of the borough's most treasured historic parks and its long musical tradition.
articles.content_html:
The sound of brass music will once again fill Hare Hill Park this autumn as the Friends of Hare Hill Park invite residents to enjoy an afternoon of live music in one of Rochdale borough's most historic green spaces.

The free concert will take place on Saturday, 6 September, from 3pm until 5pm at the park's historic bandstand, continuing a tradition of open-air performances that has entertained generations of local families. Visitors are encouraged to bring a picnic blanket or folding chair and enjoy an afternoon of music surrounded by the park's award-winning gardens.

The event has been organised by the Friends of Hare Hill Park, a volunteer-led community group established more than 14 years ago to help preserve, improve and promote the Edwardian park. During that time, the group has played a major role in securing funding, restoring historic features and ensuring the park remains one of the borough's best-loved public spaces. Their work has helped attract more than £250,000 towards restoration projects, including improvements to many of the park's original Victorian and Edwardian features. Today, Hare Hill Park proudly holds Green Flag status, recognising it as one of the country's best-managed parks.

Although often associated with Milnrow because of its close proximity, Hare Hill Park actually sits in the heart of neighbouring Littleborough. The park was created during the Victorian era alongside Hare Hill House before the estate was sold to Littleborough Urban District Council in 1900, allowing it to become the public park enjoyed by residents today.

Among its most recognisable landmarks is the Grade II-listed bandstand, presented to the people of Littleborough by local benefactor James Cryer in 1902 to commemorate the coronation of King Edward VII. More than 120 years later, it remains the centrepiece for community concerts and one of the park's most photographed historic features.

Over the decades, Hare Hill Park has welcomed countless visitors, community celebrations and civic events. The grounds have long been a venue for brass band concerts, fêtes, remembrance events, sporting activities and family gatherings, making it one of the social hearts of Littleborough and the surrounding Pennine communities.

Brass banding itself forms an important part of the area's industrial heritage. Mill towns across Lancashire and Greater Manchester developed proud brass band traditions during the nineteenth century, with local bands providing entertainment at parks, public celebrations and civic occasions. That heritage remains alive today, with Milnrow Band—founded in 1869—continuing to enjoy national success, recently earning promotion back to the prestigious British Open Championship following victory at the 2026 Grand Shield competition.

Friends of Hare Hill Park say they hope residents from across Rochdale borough will come along to enjoy an afternoon of live music while supporting the park and the volunteers who work throughout the year to keep it looking its best.

With its beautifully restored bandstand, formal gardens, mature trees and rich history, Hare Hill Park provides an ideal backdrop for a traditional brass band concert. For many visitors, it offers the chance to enjoy not only live music but one of the borough's finest historic parks, whose heritage continues to be protected by a dedicated group of local volunteers.

The concert is free to attend and takes place on Saturday, 6 September, between 3pm and 5pm.

articles.title: Milnrow author helping children cope with grief through heartfelt storybooks
articles.excerpt: Milnrow author Jane Somers is helping children understand bereavement and pet loss through two beautifully illustrated storybooks, while donating hundreds of copies to hospitals and hospices.
articles.content_html:
A Milnrow author is helping children navigate some of life's most difficult moments through a pair of beautifully illustrated books exploring bereavement and the loss of much-loved pets.

Jane Somers has written two children's books, *Look For The Robin* and *Over Rainbow Bridge*, with the aim of providing comfort, reassurance and hope for young readers experiencing grief.

Drawing on gentle storytelling and colourful illustrations, Jane's books tackle subjects that many families find difficult to discuss, helping children understand loss in an age-appropriate and compassionate way.

Her first book, *Look For The Robin*, tells the story of a friendly robin who reminds grieving children that the special people they have lost are still watching over them and that they continue to be loved. The book has resonated with families, schools and support organisations, with Jane using proceeds from sales to give something back to the community.

Thanks to the support of readers, she has now donated more than 200 copies of the book to hospitals, hospices and other worthy causes, helping children facing bereavement access the story free of charge. Customers ordering directly from her website also receive a handmade robin clay heart trinket as a keepsake.

Jane's second book, *Over Rainbow Bridge*, focuses on another form of grief that is often underestimated – the loss of a family pet. Written in rhyme and accompanied by warm illustrations, the story follows the bond between children and their beloved animals, reassuring young readers that although their pet has crossed Rainbow Bridge, the love and memories they shared remain forever.

The book aims to help parents start conversations about pet loss in a gentle, positive way, recognising that the death of a much-loved animal is often a child's first experience of bereavement. Every copy purchased through Jane's online store includes a complimentary bookmark.

Child psychologists have long recognised the importance of helping children understand grief through honest but reassuring conversations. Books can provide a safe and accessible way for young readers to explore difficult emotions, ask questions and recognise that feelings such as sadness, confusion and loss are a normal part of bereavement.

Jane says her ambition has always been to create stories that offer comfort while giving families practical tools to support children during challenging times. By combining uplifting messages with beautiful illustrations, she hopes her books provide reassurance that love continues even after someone, or a cherished pet, has gone.

Both books retail at £9.99, excluding postage and packaging, and are available directly through Jane's website. As well as supporting an independent local author, every purchase helps her continue donating copies to hospitals, hospices and organisations supporting bereaved children.

Jane's work is another example of the creativity found within Rochdale borough, using the power of storytelling not only to entertain but to make a genuine difference in the lives of local families and children across the country.

articles.title: Is this how the NHS treats its own? 81-year-old man left outside Rochdale Infirmary for ten hours
articles.excerpt: An 81-year-old man spent around ten hours lying outside Rochdale Infirmary while members of the public repeatedly sought help. Rochdale Daily investigates what happened and asks who held responsibility for his care.
articles.content_html:
An 81-year-old man lay confused, incoherent and unable to stand outside the grounds of Rochdale Infirmary for around ten hours while members of the public desperately tried to persuade the emergency services, hospital staff and social care agencies to help him.

The disturbing incident was witnessed and filmed by the editor of Rochdale Daily, who saw passers-by provide the man with water, blankets, cushions, food and cardboard while repeated attempts were made to establish which public service had responsibility for his welfare.

The man was found lying on the ground near the hospital car park. He appeared unable to stand unaided and could rarely string together more than two words. He later told those attempting to assist him that he was 81 years old.

Security staff were monitoring the situation and informed members of the public they had contacted Greater Manchester Police. Officers did not arrive until approximately ten hours after the ordeal began.

Members of the public repeatedly attempted to request an ambulance. During those calls, callers say they were informed the man was barred from the ambulance service because of previous behaviour and because of other matters that could not be discussed due to data protection legislation.

The precise legal status of any restriction involving the man has not yet been independently confirmed. However, Rochdale Daily holds video footage of the day's events, including numerous conversations between witnesses, members of the public and staff.

Whatever may have happened previously, the man lying on the ground that day appeared incapable of posing any immediate threat. He was confused, unable to stand, largely unable to communicate and repeatedly soiled himself while lying outside the hospital.

Members of the public also attempted to contact Rochdale Council Adult Social Care, people believed to be relatives, homelessness organisations and local charities. Appeals were placed on Facebook asking whether anyone knew the gentleman or could help locate family members.

Some comments on social media suggested the man had brought the situation upon himself if he had previously abused NHS staff. One commenter wrote: "You don't get barred from the NHS for nothing."

No one should minimise the abuse suffered by NHS workers. Nurses, doctors, paramedics, receptionists and security staff face unacceptable levels of violence, intimidation and verbal abuse every day. Staff deserve protection, and where individuals genuinely pose a danger, organisations are entitled to implement appropriate safeguards.

But that was not the man witnessed by Rochdale Daily.

For hour after hour he remained lying on the ground, unable to stand, struggling to communicate and apparently incapable of caring for himself. Members of the public did not witness any aggression towards staff, security or those trying to help him.

Throughout the day, ambulance vehicles entered and left the hospital site. Witnesses attempted to flag them down, but the vehicles continued past. Others reportedly stopped only to explain they were unable to assist.

Approximately six hours into the incident, two nurses accompanied by hospital security entered the car park and spoke with those attempting to help the man.

According to the editor's contemporaneous video recording, the nurses stated they could not treat the gentleman unless the situation became a matter of "life or death".

When asked what 'life or death' would look like to an untrained member of the public, they replied: "We couldn't tell you."

Members of the public then asked whose duty of care the gentleman fell under if he died while no organisation would intervene. One member of staff replied: "Not you."

When pressed as to which organisation would carry responsibility if treatment continued to be refused, those present say no clear answer was given.

One nurse then stated that the gentleman's breathing would have to stop before intervention could take place.

The editor replied that she could not see him breathing. The nurse looked over the wall towards the gentleman and responded that his chest was rising and therefore he was breathing.

During the exchange, one nurse was recorded saying: "This is what you get when you're on it day and night."

When asked what she meant by the remark, no explanation was given.

Later in the incident, a person identifying themselves as a family member stated the gentleman had dementia. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified that relationship or medical diagnosis.

A representative from Get Together After Serving CIC attended the scene after becoming aware of the incident and also attempted to secure medical assistance.

The representative said they were informed the gentleman was subject to a restraining order involving the Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust and that members of the public would need to transport him outside the area before treatment could be sought elsewhere.

Rochdale Daily has requested clarification from the Trust regarding that alleged restriction.

Throughout the ordeal, members of the public continued caring for the gentleman. Bottles of water, blankets, cushions, cardboard and food were brought to make him more comfortable while people searched desperately for someone willing to take responsibility.

Among the organisations contacted, only Get Together After Serving CIC and Hebron Pentecostal Church attended to assist.

Approximately ten hours after the incident began, police officers attended the scene.

The following morning, disposable cups, bowls and cardboard still marked the place where the elderly man had spent much of the previous day.

This investigation is not an argument that NHS staff should tolerate abuse. They should not. Nor is it an argument that previous violent or abusive behaviour should simply be ignored.

It is, however, a question of safeguarding.

If an elderly man is confused, apparently incapable of caring for himself, unable to stand, repeatedly soiling himself and lying outside the grounds of a hospital, who has responsibility for protecting him?

If previous behaviour has resulted in restrictions, what emergency pathway exists when that same individual later appears to lack capacity or requires urgent medical assessment?

Those are questions Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust, North West Ambulance Service, Greater Manchester Police and Rochdale Council's Adult Social Care service should now answer.

Rochdale Daily has contacted all relevant organisations for comment and will publish their responses in full when received.

Until then, one unavoidable question remains.

Is this how the NHS treats its own?
