articles.content_html:
Residents are being invited to discover how gardening can support wellbeing when television presenter and horticultural expert Jason Williams visits Heywood later this month for a free community event. Organised by Heywood in Bloom as part of the Great Heywood Gathering programme, the evening will explore how container gardening can improve both physical and mental wellbeing while helping people make the most of even the smallest outdoor spaces.

The event, titled 'Grow Well', will take place on Wednesday, 12 August, from 6.30pm until 9.30pm at Corcoran Close Community Room, Heywood. Organisers say refreshments will be provided free of charge, giving local residents an opportunity to meet others from the community while learning practical gardening techniques from one of the country's best-known horticultural communicators.

Jason Williams, widely known as the 'Cloud Gardener', has built a large following through his work promoting accessible gardening and encouraging people to grow flowers, fruit and vegetables in urban environments. His approach focuses on making gardening achievable for everyone, regardless of the size of their garden or outdoor space, with container gardening becoming increasingly popular among people living in flats, terraces and homes with smaller gardens.

Research continues to demonstrate the benefits gardening can have for health and wellbeing. NHS-backed social prescribing schemes increasingly include community gardening projects as a way of improving mental health, reducing loneliness, encouraging gentle physical activity and strengthening social connections. Studies have also linked time spent in green spaces with reduced stress levels and improved overall wellbeing.

The event forms part of the wider Great Heywood Gathering initiative, supported through the Culture Co-op's Creative People and Places programme. The initiative aims to bring local communities together through arts, culture, wellbeing and environmental activities, encouraging more residents to become involved in projects that improve the town and strengthen neighbourhood connections.

Heywood in Bloom has played an important role in enhancing public spaces across the town through volunteer-led planting schemes, community gardening projects and environmental improvements. Working alongside residents, schools and community organisations, the group has helped transform flower beds, public spaces and neglected areas while promoting biodiversity and civic pride.

The event has been supported by Rochdale Borough Council, Your Trust, Arts Council England, The National Lottery Community Fund and Pride in Place, reflecting the collaborative approach taken to delivering community activities across the borough.

Organisers hope the evening will inspire more people to discover the benefits of gardening, whether by growing flowers on a balcony, vegetables in containers or creating wildlife-friendly spaces at home. They also hope the event will encourage new volunteers to become involved with Heywood in Bloom and future environmental projects across the town.

Anyone interested in attending is encouraged to arrive in time for the 6.30pm start at Corcoran Close Community Room, OL10 4XD. With expert advice, free refreshments and a focus on community wellbeing, organisers hope the evening will leave attendees with practical ideas, new friendships and the confidence to start growing at home.

The café says the past month has been its most successful to date, with increasing numbers of local residents visiting for breakfast, lunch, daily specials and community activities. One of the highlights of the month was the café's World Cup Competition, organised in partnership with its sister venue, The Hive at the Million Pavilion. Together, the two cafés distributed 60 back-to-school packs to local children, helping families prepare for the new school year.

The café has also invested in additional outdoor seating, providing more space for visitors to enjoy refreshments during the warmer months. A newly introduced Book Swap Club has quickly become a popular feature, encouraging visitors to bring along books they have finished and exchange them for something new to read.

Food continues to be at the heart of the café's success. Daily specials have proved particularly popular with regular customers, while the café says its freshly prepared bacon sandwiches remain one of its biggest sellers, with demand showing no signs of slowing.

With the summer holidays now underway, The Strand Community Café has also introduced a £1.50 children's menu in a bid to provide affordable meals for local families during the school break. The initiative forms part of the café's wider commitment to ensuring the venue remains accessible to everyone in the community.

Perhaps the most unusual attraction currently drawing visitors through the doors is the café's new 'How Many Ducks?' competition. Dozens of small rubber ducks have been hidden in plain sight throughout the café, challenging customers of all ages to see how many they can spot during their visit.

The light-hearted competition has quickly become a talking point among visitors, particularly younger customers, adding another family-friendly activity alongside the café's food and community events.

In a message thanking supporters, the team said the café's success would not have been possible without the continued backing of its loyal customers, volunteers and partners. Special thanks were given to Rochdale Boroughwide Housing for placing its trust in HMR Circle – The Volunteer Drivers Service to manage the café, alongside the community hall and kitchen facilities at The Strand in Kirkholt.

The café has become more than simply a place to eat, evolving into an important community hub where residents can meet friends, enjoy affordable meals and take part in local activities. Initiatives such as the Book Swap Club, children's competitions and low-cost family meals reflect its growing role in supporting the wider Kirkholt community.

With record visitor numbers, expanding facilities and a busy programme of community initiatives, The Strand Community Café says it is looking forward to building on its success throughout the rest of the year. articles.content_html:
Every fatal road traffic collision leaves behind grieving families, devastated friends and communities asking whether more could have been done to prevent another life being cut short.

Since 2020, a number of young people have tragically lost their lives on roads across Rochdale borough. While every collision has had its own unique circumstances, each has served as a stark reminder that road safety is not simply about statistics – it is about sons, daughters, brothers, sisters, classmates and friends whose futures were taken away far too soon.

One of the most heartbreaking incidents came in April 2025 when six-year-old Myra Tahseen died after being struck by a vehicle on Ashfield Road. Emergency services fought to save her, but she sadly died from her injuries. The tragedy prompted an outpouring of grief across Rochdale, with floral tributes left at the scene and specialist officers supporting her family while investigations continued.

Although fatalities involving children and young people are thankfully rare, they remain one of the leading causes of death for those aged between five and nineteen across the United Kingdom. Rochdale's own Joint Strategic Needs Assessment highlights that land transport collisions remain among the principal causes of death for young people and reports that the borough's rate of children killed or seriously injured on the roads is around 15 per 100,000 population.

Behind every fatal collision lies a complex combination of circumstances. Excessive speed, distraction, impairment through drink or drugs, failure to wear seatbelts, poor weather, inexperience and momentary lapses in concentration can all contribute to devastating outcomes. Road safety experts consistently stress that many serious collisions are preventable through safer driving behaviour.

Young drivers remain disproportionately represented in serious road collisions nationwide. Inexperience, overconfidence and risk-taking behaviour can all increase the likelihood of being involved in a collision, particularly during the first years after passing a driving test. Equally, young pedestrians and cyclists are among the most vulnerable road users, particularly near schools, residential estates and busy roads.

Greater Manchester Police's Serious Collision Investigation Unit continues to investigate every fatal collision thoroughly, examining witness statements, CCTV, vehicle data, road conditions and forensic evidence to establish exactly what happened. These investigations often continue for many months before an inquest is held, allowing families to receive answers and, where appropriate, criminal proceedings to take place.

Road safety is not solely the responsibility of drivers. Pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists and passengers all have a role to play in reducing risk. Simple decisions such as slowing down in residential areas, putting mobile phones away, wearing seatbelts correctly, using pedestrian crossings where available and remaining alert around schools can make a significant difference.

Across Rochdale borough, organisations continue to work together to improve road safety through engineering improvements, education campaigns, enforcement against dangerous driving and community awareness initiatives. Every serious collision provides lessons that can help prevent future tragedies.

For the families who have lost loved ones, however, those lessons come at an unimaginable cost. Birthdays go uncelebrated, empty seats remain at family tables and communities continue to remember young lives that ended far too soon.

The hope shared by police, road safety campaigners and residents alike is that by learning from these tragedies, encouraging responsible driving and remaining vigilant on every journey, fewer families will have to experience the heartbreak of losing someone they love on Rochdale's roads.

articles.title: Veterans charity says demand for support is growing after emotional day for volunteers
articles.excerpt: A Rochdale organisation supporting military veterans and disadvantaged young people has issued an emotional appeal for greater support after a recent case reminded volunteers why their work remains so important.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale-based community organisation supporting military veterans and disadvantaged young people has issued an emotional appeal for greater public support after what it described as one of the most challenging days in its history.

Get Together After Serving CIC (GTAS) said a recent case involving people it was assisting left members of its leadership team deeply affected, highlighting the growing pressures facing both former servicemen and women and vulnerable children within the community. While the organisation has not released details of the case in order to protect those involved, it says the experience reinforced the urgent need for the support services it provides every day.

In a heartfelt statement shared with supporters, GTAS explained that one of its directors, Wayne, was left visibly emotional after witnessing the circumstances surrounding the latest referral. According to the organisation, despite a lifetime of experience dealing with trauma, military service and personal hardship, the situation served as a powerful reminder that many people continue to struggle in silence.

The organisation says these moments rarely become public. Instead, staff and volunteers often work quietly behind the scenes, providing practical assistance, emotional support and signposting to those who find themselves in crisis. GTAS says much of its work takes place away from social media and public attention, with the focus remaining firmly on helping individuals rather than seeking recognition.

Founded to support former members of the Armed Forces while also creating opportunities for disadvantaged children and young people, Get Together After Serving CIC has steadily expanded its role within the local community. Alongside offering companionship and welfare support for veterans, the organisation works to reduce social isolation, improve wellbeing and create positive opportunities for young people who may otherwise feel overlooked.

Veterans' charities across the UK have repeatedly highlighted the complex challenges many former service personnel face after leaving the Armed Forces. Although the transition to civilian life is smooth for many, others experience difficulties relating to housing, employment, mental health, financial hardship or adjusting to life outside military service. Community organisations often play an important role by offering early intervention before problems escalate.

At the same time, many charities supporting children and young people have reported increasing demand for services as families continue to face financial pressures and wider social challenges. Community groups such as GTAS frequently rely on volunteers, donations and fundraising to continue delivering projects that might otherwise be unavailable to those who need them.

GTAS says its work demonstrates how relatively small organisations can have a significant impact despite operating with limited resources. Its latest appeal emphasises that a dedicated team of volunteers continues to provide support every day because they believe nobody should have to face hardship alone.

In its statement, the organisation said the latest events reinforced its belief that its work is not simply beneficial but, in some cases, life-changing. It described helping veterans find safety and dignity while giving disadvantaged young people opportunities, stability and a place where they feel valued.

The charity is now encouraging local residents, businesses and community organisations to become involved, whether by volunteering, making donations, fundraising or simply helping raise awareness of its work. It believes that increasing community support will allow it to reach more people before problems become crises.

Like many community interest companies, GTAS operates in an increasingly challenging funding environment. Demand for grassroots support services has grown while competition for grants and charitable funding has become more intense. As a result, many organisations rely heavily on local goodwill to sustain their work.

The latest appeal serves as a reminder that behind every public fundraising campaign or social media post are real people facing difficult circumstances, often away from public view. For the volunteers involved, success is not measured by headlines or recognition but by the number of people who receive help when they need it most.

Anyone wishing to learn more about Get Together After Serving CIC, volunteer their time or support its work can find further information through the organisation's social media channels. GTAS says every contribution, no matter how small, helps strengthen its ability to support veterans and young people across the Rochdale area.

articles.title: Residents voice concerns over dangerous driving and alleged street racing on Milkstone Road
articles.excerpt: Residents have raised concerns about dangerous driving and alleged street racing on Milkstone Road, with calls for stronger enforcement to improve road safety.
articles.content_html:
Residents and business owners along Milkstone Road are continuing to raise concerns about dangerous driving, excessive speeding and alleged late-night street racing, with many calling for stronger enforcement before someone is seriously injured.

Milkstone Road is one of Rochdale's busiest routes, carrying thousands of vehicles each day while also serving local shops, schools, places of worship and residential streets. For many residents, the road should be a safe route for families, pedestrians and cyclists. However, some say that during evenings and late at night, it can become the scene of drivers accelerating aggressively, revving engines and travelling at excessive speeds.

While there is no evidence to suggest organised street racing is a regular occurrence, residents have reported vehicles appearing to race one another, performing rapid acceleration and driving in a manner they believe is dangerous. Such behaviour can create significant risks for other motorists, pedestrians and nearby residents, particularly on a road with numerous junctions, crossings and side streets.

The concerns reflect a wider national problem. Police forces across the country have stepped up action against illegal street racing and antisocial driving, warning that the behaviour can have devastating consequences. The Government has also strengthened powers allowing police to seize and destroy vehicles used in antisocial driving offences in appropriate circumstances.

Road safety already forms one of the priorities for Greater Manchester Police's Milkstone and Deeplish neighbourhood team. Officers say they are carrying out high-visibility traffic operations, speed enforcement and action against inconsiderate motorists alongside wider work tackling antisocial behaviour and organised crime in the area.

Residents say the issue extends beyond noise. High-speed driving can intimidate pedestrians, discourage people from walking to local businesses and increase the risk of collisions. Milkstone Road is a busy mixed-use corridor where children, elderly residents and shoppers regularly cross the road throughout the day.

National road safety experts have consistently warned that excessive speed dramatically reduces the time available for drivers to react while increasing both the likelihood and severity of collisions. Even where no crash occurs, repeated antisocial driving can have a lasting impact on neighbourhoods through noise, fear and disruption.

Many local residents are now calling for additional measures, including increased police patrols during evening hours, more targeted traffic enforcement, mobile speed checks and continued action against drivers found to be driving dangerously or inconsiderately.

Greater Manchester Police encourages anyone witnessing dangerous driving to report it where it is safe to do so. Dashcam footage, CCTV and details such as registration numbers, locations and times can all assist officers in identifying offenders. Residents should always call 999 if they believe there is an immediate danger to life or serious risk to road users.

For most drivers, Milkstone Road is simply another journey home or to work. However, residents hope that continued enforcement and responsible driving will ensure the road remains safe for everyone who lives, works and travels through one of Rochdale's busiest neighbourhoods.

articles.title: Litter blighting Deeplish remains a concern for residents
articles.excerpt: Residents are calling for continued action to tackle litter in Deeplish, with many saying cleaner streets would improve community pride and the appearance of the neighbourhood.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Deeplish are continuing to raise concerns about litter on streets, pavements and alleyways, with many saying more needs to be done to improve the appearance of one of Rochdale's busiest neighbourhoods.

Discarded food packaging, drinks containers, household waste and fly-tipped rubbish have become a familiar sight in some parts of the area, particularly around shopping parades, rear alleyways and heavily used pedestrian routes. While council cleansing teams regularly clear litter and remove illegally dumped waste, many residents say the problem often returns within days.

Litter is more than just an eyesore. Environmental experts warn that rubbish left on streets can block drains, attract vermin, harm wildlife and negatively affect people's perception of their neighbourhood. Research has also suggested that cleaner streets can help improve community pride and reduce further anti-social behaviour.

Rochdale Borough Council says it has enforcement officers patrolling the borough who can issue £75 fixed penalty notices to anyone caught dropping litter. The authority is also responsible for removing litter from public land, emptying public bins and responding to reports of overflowing bins and fly-tipping. Residents can report litter, overflowing bins and illegally dumped waste through the council's online reporting system.

In recent years, the council has also carried out targeted environmental improvement projects in the wider Milkstone and Deeplish ward. These have included deep-cleaning operations, alleyway clearances, vegetation removal and educational campaigns encouraging residents to dispose of waste responsibly. Environmental officers have also visited homes to provide advice on recycling, bulky waste collections and proper waste disposal.

Those projects have delivered visible improvements in some locations. Previous council feedback found many residents believed streets were noticeably cleaner following targeted clean-up initiatives, although some also suggested additional litter bins and continued maintenance would help sustain those improvements.

Community groups say keeping Deeplish clean is a shared responsibility. While enforcement and regular cleansing remain important, they argue lasting improvements depend on residents, businesses and visitors disposing of rubbish responsibly and reporting fly-tipping when it occurs.

The council also supports volunteer litter-picking groups by providing equipment and arranging the collection of rubbish gathered during organised clean-up events, allowing local people to play an active role in improving their neighbourhood.

Many residents believe Deeplish has a strong community spirit and deserves clean, welcoming streets that reflect the pride people take in the area. They hope continued enforcement against littering, regular cleansing operations and greater public awareness will help ensure that progress made through previous environmental improvement projects is not undone.

Anyone who witnesses littering or discovers fly-tipped waste on public land is encouraged to report it to Rochdale Borough Council, helping officers identify problem areas and take enforcement action where appropriate.

articles.title: Bill Oddie Reflects on Rochdale Roots in BBC Documentary
articles.excerpt: Bill Oddie, the star of The Goodies and Springwatch, explored his Rochdale heritage in a recent episode of Who Do You Think You Are?, revealing family history and personal insights.
articles.content_html:
Bill Oddie, the renowned television personality known for his work on The Goodies and Springwatch, recently revisited his Rochdale roots in an episode of the BBC series Who Do You Think You Are?. Born in 1941 at Birch Hill Hospital in Littleborough, Oddie moved away from Rochdale at the age of seven when his father secured a job in Birmingham.

During the documentary, Oddie discovered that his ancestors were predominantly mill workers. He learned that his grandmother, Emily Worrall, who played a significant role in his upbringing, was born in Rochdale and likely worked at Arrow Mill in Castleton from the age of 13. Oddie reflected on his complicated relationship with his father, attributing it to his grandmother's influence, while also acknowledging her impact on his passion for birds.

The programme also shed light on Oddie's mother, Lilian, who was committed to a psychiatric institution during his childhood. He had long believed she suffered from schizophrenia and had abandoned him, but he later learned from nurses that she was actually a manic depressive. Oddie's mother had experienced significant trauma, including the loss of a daughter shortly before his birth, which he had not fully understood until now.

Oddie expressed that this journey into his family's past has been transformative, allowing him to reassess his feelings towards his mother. He stated, "This journey has been a real lifesaver... I wish I'd known her better and I wish she'd known me." His reflections highlight the complexities of familial relationships and the impact of understanding one's history.

articles.title: Middleton protest planned as organiser sets out bail conditions ahead of event
articles.excerpt: A protest is planned in Middleton Gardens on 8 August, with organiser Jamie Thomason outlining his intended arrangements and referring to bail conditions while police are expected to oversee the event.
articles.content_html:
A public protest is due to take place in Middleton Gardens on Saturday, 8 August, with organiser Jamie Thomason stating he intends to comply with his bail conditions while addressing supporters before leaving the area. According to a statement published on social media, Greater Manchester Police will have officers present during the event, with police liaison officers said to be aware of the arrangements.

In his announcement, Thomason said he would be joined by several guest speakers from across the UK, including Ashlea Simon of All for England, Dorothy Jones and Pag Billy UK, with additional speakers yet to be confirmed. He described his planned speech as being based on information which he says can be verified through publicly available sources and encouraged supporters to attend the demonstration.

Thomason also referred to his current bail conditions, stating that he is prohibited from congregating with more than ten people. He asked supporters not to approach him in groups, saying he had agreed with Greater Manchester Police that he would attend, deliver his speech and leave Middleton immediately afterwards. He also stated that he would give his speech from a distance and would not become involved in any confrontation because he did not intend to breach his bail conditions.

Rochdale Daily has not independently verified the specific bail conditions referred to in Thomason's post, and reports them only as claims made by the organiser himself.

The right to peaceful protest is protected in UK law under Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, although that right is subject to restrictions where they are lawful, necessary and proportionate. Police have powers under the Public Order Act 1986, as amended by more recent legislation including the Public Order Act 2023, to impose conditions on public assemblies where they reasonably believe serious public disorder, serious disruption, intimidation or damage may occur. Participants are expected to comply with any lawful conditions imposed.

Greater Manchester Police has previously stated that its role at public demonstrations is to facilitate peaceful and lawful protest while taking action where criminal offences are committed or where public safety is at risk. Depending on the circumstances, officers may deploy protest liaison teams, public order officers or other resources to manage events and minimise disruption to the wider community.

The planned demonstration is likely to attract differing opinions from residents. Supporters say the event is intended to raise awareness of issues they believe are affecting communities across the country, while others are expected to disagree with both the organisers and the views expressed. Peaceful disagreement and lawful protest are protected rights, provided they remain within the limits of the law.

Anyone travelling through Middleton town centre on Saturday should be aware that there may be an increased police presence around Middleton Gardens while the demonstration takes place. At the time of publication, no official road closures, dispersal orders or protest conditions had been publicly announced.

Rochdale Daily has contacted Greater Manchester Police for comment to confirm the policing arrangements for the event, including whether officers will be deployed, whether any conditions have been imposed under public order legislation, and whether any road closures, dispersal powers or other measures are anticipated. This article will be updated if and when a response is received.

articles.title: Residents urged to attend Greenvale planning meeting as decision nears
articles.excerpt: Campaigners are encouraging residents to attend Rochdale Borough Council's Planning Committee as councillors prepare to consider the Greenvale planning application for land south of Greenvale in Bamford.
articles.content_html:
Residents opposed to the proposed Greenvale development in Bamford are being encouraged to attend next week's Planning Committee meeting, where councillors are expected to consider the application for housing on land south of Greenvale. Campaigners say a strong public turnout will demonstrate the level of local concern surrounding the proposal.

The application, reference 25/00405/FUL, is listed as Item 7 on the agenda for Rochdale Borough Council's Planning Committee meeting on Wednesday, 5 August. The meeting is scheduled to begin at 6pm, with the Greenvale application expected to be considered during the evening.

The appeal has been organised by the Bamford Green Belt Action Group and supported by the Save Bamford Greenbelt campaign, which has urged residents to attend the meeting regardless of whether they intend to speak. In a public appeal, campaigners said simply being present would help demonstrate to committee members how important the decision is to the local community.

Campaigners argue there remain significant planning policy and evidence gaps which should be addressed before any decision is taken. They believe the proposed development would result in the unnecessary loss of Green Belt land and have consistently maintained that the site should remain protected from development.

The Green Belt surrounding Bamford has been the subject of longstanding debate as Rochdale Borough Council seeks to balance housing demand with the protection of open countryside. Supporters of Green Belt protection argue the land plays an important role in preventing urban sprawl, preserving the character of existing communities and providing valuable green space for wildlife and recreation. Those in favour of development argue additional housing is needed to meet growing demand and support future economic growth.

Planning Committee members are required to determine applications based on planning law and adopted planning policy rather than the popularity of a proposal. Material planning considerations can include matters such as highway safety, flood risk, ecology, landscape impact, heritage, design and compliance with local and national planning policies. Issues such as the identity of an applicant or the level of public support alone are not determinative, although representations submitted by residents are taken into account where they raise relevant planning matters.

Residents wishing to observe the meeting can attend in person, while those who have registered in advance may be permitted to address the committee in accordance with the council's procedures. Anyone intending to speak should check Rochdale Borough Council's guidance on registration deadlines and speaking arrangements before the meeting.

The committee's decision will determine whether planning permission is granted, refused or deferred pending further information. Whatever the outcome, the decision is expected to be closely watched by residents across Bamford and neighbouring communities, where the future of Green Belt land continues to generate strong public interest.
